Context: In this magazine article, the author interviews astronomer Edward Ashton.
Title: Edward Ashton, Astronomer
Author: by Nick D'Alto
Content: The astronomer who led the team behind the impressive `text(Saturn)` moon discovery was Edward Ashton...
Finding all these new moons wasn't exactly an overnight discovery. What was the process like?
It certainly wasn't a quick discovery. I started this research almost `text(five years)` ago.
We used data taken using ... a `text(3.6-meter)` [`text(10.5-foot)`] optical/infrared telescope... The images we used were taken over many `text(three-hour)` periods, between `2019` and `2021`.

While these were superb images, these moons were still too faint to see in them. So, we used special techniques, such as `text(one)` called shift and stack, to overlap the images and merge the data together, to make the moons visible.
Then seeing all those tiny dots around `text(Saturn)` was the aha moment?

Not yet. Just finding an object close to a planet doesn't guarantee it's a moon. It could be an asteroid passing near the planet. Also, objects near a planet don't always remain there. To be sure, we must track an object for several `text(years)`, to prove that it's really orbiting the planet. It's a very formalized process.

Have you ever played a game of connect the dots? It was a little like that. We had to connect where an object that we thought was a moon appeared in many different images. So, we could piece together how that object might be orbiting around the planet. At times, it was like playing a `text(hundred)` games of connect the dots — on the same page. But without knowing which dot belonged to which puzzle!
Had any of these moons been seen before?

In fact, some of them had been spotted briefly many `text(years)` ago but hadn't been tracked long enough to prove that they traveled around the planet in stable orbits. This is easy to understand, because these moons all orbit very far from the planet...
Isn't it tough to keep track of them?

It is tough. `text(First)`, we needed to screen out `text(Saturn's)` already-known moons. Plus, we had to submit our findings to the Minor Planet Center, which keeps track of these kinds of natural satellites. And their archives of past sightings go back many `text(years)`. So, once we knew our orbits, we had to run those orbits backwards in time, to see if any of our finds matched the old records. When we did find a match, that was extra proof.
`text(Saturn)` is almost a `text(billion miles)` from the sun, yet you were able to find small moons!

Yes, `text(each moon)` we found is in the range of about `text(two)` to `text(three)` miles [`3.2` to `text(4.8 kilometers)`] across. These moons are about as small as current technology can detect, at that range. And that's important. It reminds us that our solar system is really a collection of objects, but greatly varying scales.
